questions.q: What is an ecosystem?
questions.a: All interacting organisms in an area together with their physical surroundings - the biotic and abiotic parts working as one unit.

questions.q: Name the two components of an ecosystem.
questions.a: Biotic (living organisms) and abiotic (temperature, light, water, soil) components.

questions.q: Give an example of a natural and an artificial ecosystem.
questions.a: Natural: forest, pond, lake; artificial: aquarium, crop field, garden.

questions.q: What are producers, consumers and decomposers?
questions.a: Producers make food from sunlight (green plants); consumers eat other organisms; decomposers break down dead matter into soil nutrients.

questions.q: Why are decomposers essential in nature?
questions.a: They recycle nutrients back to the soil and clear away dead bodies and waste.

questions.q: Classify a rabbit, a grass plant and fungi.
questions.a: Grass is a producer, rabbit a (primary) consumer, fungi a decomposer.

questions.q: What is a food chain?
questions.a: A sequence showing who eats whom - energy passing from producers through successive consumers.

questions.q: Why are food chains limited to 3-4 trophic levels?
questions.a: Only 10% of energy transfers at each step, so little energy remains after a few levels to support more.

questions.q: What is a food web?
questions.a: Many interconnected food chains in an ecosystem, since most organisms eat more than one kind of food.

concepts.title: The Ten Percent Law of Energy Transfer

solution_steps.name: level2
solution_steps.explain: only 10% passes to the next trophic level

questions.q: Plants trap 10000 kJ of energy. Using the ten per cent law, how much reaches the tertiary consumer?
questions.a: 10 kJ

questions.q: If producers hold 50000 kJ, how much energy flows to the third trophic level of consumers (carnivore level)?
questions.a: 50 kJ

questions.q: A grassland stores 2000 kJ in grass. What energy is available to a snake four steps up the food chain?
questions.a: 2 kJ

questions.q: Algae fix 8000 kJ. Compute the energy at the fourth trophic level.
questions.a: 8 kJ

questions.q: With 1000 kJ trapped by trees, how much reaches a top carnivore?
questions.a: 1 kJ

Incident sunlight of 500000 kJ: find the producer-trapped share and the herbivore share.
questions.a: 500 kJ

questions.q: A pond receives 2000000 kJ of sunlight. Compute the energy fixed by algae and that reaching zooplankton.
On 250000 kJ of sunlight, what energy do plants fix and what do grazers receive?
questions.a: 250 kJ

questions.q: A forest intercepts 100000 kJ of sun energy. How much is available at the producer and herbivore levels?
questions.a: 100 kJ

questions.q: What is biological magnification?
questions.a: Non-biodegradable pesticides grow more concentrated at each trophic level, harming top consumers most.

questions.q: Why are humans most affected by pesticide magnification?
questions.a: Humans sit at the top of many food chains, so accumulated pesticides concentrate highest in us.

questions.q: Why can't pesticide levels fall in a food chain once sprayed?
questions.a: The chemicals are non-biodegradable - they are not broken down and keep passing up the chain, accumulating in body fat.

questions.q: How is ozone formed in the upper atmosphere?
questions.a: UV radiation splits O2 into free oxygen atoms, which combine with O2 molecules to form ozone (O3).

questions.q: What is the importance of the ozone layer?
questions.a: It absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation from the sun, shielding living beings from skin damage and cancer.

questions.q: Which chemicals damage the ozone layer and how?
questions.a: CFCs release chlorine atoms in the stratosphere that break ozone molecules, thinning the layer.
